fieldsRead.programmeDescription: Islam, Politics and Society at Radboud studies Islamic traditions, sacred texts and the lives of Muslim communities in historical and contemporary contexts. Students combine religious studies with social and political inquiry.
fieldsRead.comparisonExplanation: The adopted curriculum is shown below as a supported outline while course entry requirements are being checked. UCR alternatives are withheld until that check is complete. The reviewed UCR courses offer related study in philosophy, politics, social research and cultural heritage, but a final comparability decision has not been approved.

curriculum.routeLabel: Full bachelor without Arabic: requirements check pending
curriculum.limitation: The adopted curriculum lists 180 EC: 120 EC of required major study, two whole 15 EC modules and 30 EC of open minor study. A prior-knowledge condition in Religion in the Public Domain still needs clarification for this route. This is a supported outline, not a certified complete pathway. Introductory instruction and the academic Dutch assessment carry no credits.

componentNotes.y2-module: Selected 15 EC restricted module: religious and moral meanings of care, religious texts and rituals in healthcare, and psychology of religion. Other whole-module choices are permitted.
componentNotes.y3-module: Selected 15 EC restricted module: religion, humans and nature; integral ecology; and climate change in the global South. Other whole-module choices are permitted.
componentNotes.minor-space: 30 EC of open bachelor study, with no overlap. Advance approval applies to relevant outside-faculty choices and internships.
componentNotes.y2-research: Year-long methods and research project building on first-year methods and skills.
componentNotes.y3-thesis: 10 EC of independent research with academic skills prior knowledge, compulsory workshop attendance, approval of the research question and individual supervision.
componentNotes.y1-islamic-thought: Required 5 EC on Islamic philosophy, theology, law and mysticism. The current course imposes no entry prerequisite. Introductory Islam knowledge is expected, with optional introductory videos available. Assessment includes active participation, reading questions and a written exam.
componentNotes.y2-public: The current catalogue requires prior knowledge of Buddhism and Hinduism. How that condition is met in this pathway still needs confirmation.

preparedDescriptionReviews.text: Law, Society & Justice examines legal, social and normative perspectives on law. Students compare legal traditions and study public and private law, human rights, justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, demand letters and mock trials develop legal reasoning, while a family-law topic supports the design of a socio-legal research proposal.

preparedDescriptionReviews.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
preparedDescriptionReviews.text:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century.


Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants.


This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.

An experience report connects engagement or observation to course concepts, while an individual project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyse a civil-society organisation, movement or initiative.

preparedDescriptionReviews.text: Media & Race investigates storytelling, power, privilege, resistance and systemic racism in American history from the late nineteenth century to the present. Film, photographs, music and other media connect past and present. Students produce research-based podcasts exploring how media sustains oppression and supports resistance.

preparedDescriptionReviews.text: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.

preparedDescriptionReviews.name: Writing Art's Histories
preparedDescriptionReviews.text: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
